excerpt: This appears the first decision AI that actually handles audio, video, and PDF, and I'm surprised this isn't highlighted everywhere.

This appears the first decision AI that actually handles audio, video, and PDF, and I'm surprised this isn't highlighted everywhere.

Marketing seems to have dropped the ball on that. I doubt anyone's picking it for the +2% higher points, but being able to answer based on a PDF or call is groundbreaking.

Jev is still faster and cheaper for many of the common text uses.


>Marketing seems to have dropped the ball on that

Google's marketing consistently drops the ball on every opportunity so that's not surprising at all


I'm sort of surprised it took Jev for everyone to realize "oh yeah, this is a useful thing that we should have in our product portfolio".

But maybe this is one of those things that's only obvious in retrospect? I'm sure people were trying something similar years ago with grammar-constrained outputs (for example to only output a simple json structure), but you can't get probabilities out of the model that way. Which makes me wonder: how do these models calculate probabilities?


A lot of AI stuff is like that, actually. GPT 2 and 3 were mainly curiosities that would get articles on tech news sites but didn’t attract much attention from the general public. But after RLHF the UX improved dramatically and ChatGPT became mainstream. A lot of MLEs underestimate how much UX matters, and the same is true for Jev.

> how do these models calculate probabilities?

The short answer is: more and better data.

The long answer is: probably the same way any other classifier does. Take your ground truth probabilities and your predicted probabilities. The gap between those is called cross entropy, which is used to push the model towards the correct probabilities.


> which is used to push the model towards the correct probabilities.

The definition of "correct probability" here is usually "p=1 for the ground truth label, p=0 for all others." Which seems like an intuitive approach but if you actually think about it doesn't trivially imply the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty.


Wouldn't learning a calibrated probability distribution just be a consequence of the CE loss being a proper scoring rule? So, by construction, they are approximating the distribution of the labels. Of course in practice there might be issues with overfitting the log-likelihood and the with the labels being a finite sample of the population distribution


Yes, in a sense, with some important caveats. Cross-entropy will tend to yield reasonable marginal (i.e., not class-wise, not approximately conditional) calibration for in-distribution (i.i.d. data). The challenge with LMs, and neural networks more generally, is that the resulting estimators that are based on the output logits are very brittle to covariate shifts and out-of-distribution data, and that for real applications, we often need robust estimates in high-probability regions (e.g., of class- and prediction-conditional accuracy at least some value near 1) for conditional-branching decisions (by a human or a model). (ECE is the wrong metric for that quantity.)

The various decision APIs don't give you that, and would themselves need to be recalibrated with constraints in feature-representation space over the applicable reference class, as with https://pypi.org/project/reexpress-sdm/.


For a single prediction, sure. But the model doesn't make a single prediction and then stop existing. It makes an unbounded number of future predictions and under that assumption it is reasonable to expect the model to behave optimally under Bayes rule - which has a unique global minimizer at E[(Y-F(X))^2].

So counter to your claim that "It doesn't trivially imply that the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty" I think you need to consider what it means to optimally update a posterior under the global minimizer of the true conditional distribution.


The thing I had to wrap my head around is: For a "classic" classifier, the classes are fixed and the data distribution is p(x,y). The calibration is checked over this single distribution. Jev makes the tasks part of the input, so the data distribution is p(task,x,y) and calibration is averaged over that joint distribution. What follows is that while for classic classifiers, calibration brakes down if your x was out-of-distribution, it can now also break if your task is out of distribution. The big question now is: Can subtle differences in phrasing your task already lead to this? And the only way to verify calibration is having ground truth data to validate on. Also: Calibration over p(task, x, y) means calibrated on average across tasks. Even an in-distribution task can be over- or underconfident while the average looks fine.


> And the only way to verify calibration is having ground truth data to validate on

I’m not sure that’s true in real cases.

I would expect that in distribution tasks have quite consistent outcomes with variations on phrasing. I would expect that to be much less true when tasks are out of distribution. So could we randomly adjust phrasing and see how much the results change - looking less for truth but consistency?


A model can be consistently over- or under-confident for similar inputs. The only way to check if it's actually calibrated is to compare against some known ground truth. I don't see any way around that.


In my experience, calibration is only ever in expectation, even for a classic classifier. Any given prediction is often still over- or under-confident.


> It makes an unbounded number of future predictions

nit: it's trained on finitely many samples.

> So counter to your claim that "It doesn't trivially imply that the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty" I think you need to consider what it means to optimally update a posterior under the global minimizer of the true conditional distribution.

Huh? That's not counter to anything I said. All I said was it's not trivially implied.

But instead of producing a completion it fills in the schema. But it’s always - “given the context, the schema needs to be filled in like this”

Basically there is a whole host of tarpit usage of LLMs in application backends today. This is simply another case of LLMs enabling people to build what they cannot productionize or maintain.

Today developers without any AI/ML skillset can prototype a fancy new feature with LLMs, what used to require collecting and curating data to train a pipeline of ML models then serving them in production.

The problem comes when it's time to take the new feature into production. That $20 cost with prototype/beta workload is now $30k per month in LLM costs, and those hallucinations that never happened on their 200 test samples is happening 600 times per day.

They are then stuck, because they lack the knowledge and budget to build and run the production ML pipeline properly, the infra stack necessary to handle production workload. Management also doesn't understand why they have to invest in rebuilding something that "seems to work" with "outdated methods".

These system one or decision models are a step up from LLMs when it comes to this usage. Problem is that they are still difficult to work with (limited in expression power) for many application logic. Despite the initial popularity, I hear about a lot of frictions refactoring LLM based backend with them, and multiple cases of production rollbacks to LLMs already.

I think system one models is a sensible paradigm, but there is a lot more work needed above the model layer to make this work.


That also makes me wonder: what other things are achieved by now and are up for grabs, and that will seem obvious in retrospect, but we don't notice it yet?

Roughly speaking, has AGI actually been achieved two years ago and we go around don't noticing that?


> Which makes me wonder: how do these models calculate probabilities?

By unprincipled methods. To calibrate confidence in an answer you need a task specific calibration set. You can't pre-calibrate for tasks unknown ahead of time, which is the case for most uses of decision models.


In some sense everything an LLM does is by unprincipled methods. But it works! We judge it empirically post hoc by its performance rather than relying on tuning.

Hell, human thinking is unprincipled in basically the exact same way.


We were doing zero and few-shot classification with LLMs since before they could reliably complete whole sentences. It’s an easier task than generating coherent text. The model needed to be tuned for classification (not generation) and for the domain, but it would often succeed at new classification tasks with a simple description.

I guess given the huge advances in LLM since then, these models probably achieve much better accuracy on a wide range of domains with lower effort compared to what we were doing, which makes it compelling as a product. And yeah, the models probably were already good enough a few years ago too. Other factors include how easy it is to release products at high speed now, and the desire in the industry to reduce token spend.

Decision models are really not much different than that, but (usually) scaled up to bigger causal models.

If you are looking to do Jev-like things with smaller models, check into NLI.

Every time I see someone saying something like "isn't this just structured output?", it's because they don't understand that probability calibration is one of the most important parts of the product, especially to understand uncertainty.

I think Jev did a pretty good job on calibration. I wonder how the fast-follow competition from OpenAI and Gemini do.


Right, that's always been true for LLMs + constrained generation. It ensures syntactic correctness, but semantics are "best effort".


Not reliably - look at microsoft's guidance project that did some of this.

Once a model goes through instruction fine tuning and RLVR/RLHF the log probs decorrelate from what's ground truth (given the propensity of the data seen during training)


But I assume it wouldn't take much more training to make them good again - just a matter of picking the right loss function, since this sort of stuff is probably all encoded in the last layer or two anyway.

Task classification - given a set of classes, return the most likely class for each task

Guardrails - check the text against a set of guardrail checks (questions)

Search - Given a search criteria, I first have an LLM generate a query that would go to the decision model. This query is a rubric that scores each document. The highest scoring documents become the search hits. This is fast and cheap, so you can use it as a cross-encoder for your entire set, instead of just as a final re-ranker.

Image input is a primary reason I've never moved off my "home rolled" version of Jev (that Claude wrote for me over a year ago) for my file organizer/indexer. Takes images resizes them to 1k, then asks a handful of questions about the image for tagging purposes. It is able to process around 3 images a second based on Qwen 3 VL, but distilled and optimized for 1k images and up to 2048 token inputs (after the system prompt, then the questions are asked one after each other reusing the cache). Documents that are longer than that end up going through a summarizer that runs on my other GPU (Qwen 3.6, I think). And all of that gets fed into a vector search engine, for easy lookup later.

I'm not even sure what all is going on inside it anymore, because I just add new features when they popup, and tell Claude to do it, and it let's me know when it is done, and every new "input feature" can run against the entire catalogue of files.

It makes an unbounded number of future predictions and under that assumption it is reasonable to expect the model to behave optimally under Bayes rule - which has a unique global minimizer at E[(Y-F(X))^2].So counter to your claim that "It doesn't trivially imply that the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty" I think you need to consider what it means to optimally update a posterior under the global minimizer of the true conditional distribution. The thing I had to wrap my head around is: For a "classic" classifier, the classes are fixed and the data distribution is p(x,y). The calibration is checked over this single distribution. Jev makes the tasks part of the input, so the data distribution is p(task,x,y) and calibration is averaged over that joint distribution. What follows is that while for classic classifiers, calibration brakes down if your x was out-of-distribution, it can now also break if your task is out of distribution. The big question now is: Can subtle differences in phrasing your task already lead to this? And the only way to verify calibration is having ground truth data to validate on. Also: Calibration over p(task, x, y) means calibrated on average across tasks. Even an in-distribution task can be over- or underconfident while the average looks fine. > And the only way to verify calibration is having ground truth data to validate onI’m not sure that’s true in real cases.I would expect that in distribution tasks have quite consistent outcomes with variations on phrasing. I would expect that to be much less true when tasks are out of distribution. So could we randomly adjust phrasing and see how much the results change - looking less for truth but consistency? A model can be consistently over- or under-confident for similar inputs. The only way to check if it's actually calibrated is to compare against some known ground truth. I don't see any way around that. In my experience, calibration is only ever in expectation, even for a classic classifier. Any given prediction is often still over- or under-confident. > It makes an unbounded number of future predictionsnit: it's trained on finitely many samples.> So counter to your claim that "It doesn't trivially imply that the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty" I think you need to consider what it means to optimally update a posterior under the global minimizer of the true conditional distribution.Huh? That's not counter to anything I said. All I said was it's not trivially implied. From what I’ve gathered, it doesn’t work at all like a normal classifier. As in, for a classifier you’d train it for a specific task to reduce the cross entropy. So, in a hand-wavy way “the model knows the truth”. For Jev-type models it’s more like an LLM, in the sense that the “truth” is in the context you provide. But instead of producing a completion it fills in the schema. But it’s always - “given the context, the schema needs to be filled in like this” as s.o. who registered their chatgpt account on the third day after they released, I can tell you chatgpt actually became mainstream overnight. > A lot of AI stuff is like that, actually.Chain of thought was that way. DeepSeek came out, and not long thereafter everyone had adopted chain of thought. Unless I am misunderstanding you then I don't think this is correct. Chain of thought was first proposed in 2022. Assuming you mean reasoning models then the correct comparison is GPT-o1, which came out in September 2024, 2 months prior to R1 lite preview. In the next 2 months, prior to the release of the full R1 model, both qwen and gemini released reasoning models. Dario explicitly notes in early 2025 that most major labs had been working on reasoning models in 2024, and explicitly credits OAI for pulling things forward with their release.https://darioamodei.com/post/on-deepseek-and-export-controls> In 2024, the idea of using reinforcement learning (RL) to train models to generate chains of thought has become a new focus of scaling. Anthropic, DeepSeek, and many other companies (perhaps most notably OpenAI who released their o1-preview model in September) have found that this training greatly increases performance on certain select, objectively measurable tasks like math, coding competitions, and on reasoning that resembles these tasks. CoT is far older than DeepSeek.I remember adding it to GPT-3.0 and getting a big boost in accuracy. It was like magic.And then we would handcraft thoughts and inject that into the prompt so the model thinks its owns thoughts and would follow instructions much more precisely.This was well before reasoning models, even before chat models. I wasn't suggesting they invented it. I was suggesting that they popularized it, made a huge amount of noise about it, and it seemed like after they did, there was a lot more attention on it. I think if you were paying attention at the time, CoT and ReAct loops were already "well known". Lots of GPT wrappers at the time were doing it, I remember doing CoT to help measure the calories for a recipe. The problem is tokens then were quite expensive and doing experimentation on it was pretty expensive for an individual. I once accidentally spent $20 trying to categorize a Who's Hiring post from here lol.It was a short-lived time though. I think only a few months before Deepseek really RLed the reasoning which produced much better reasoning than just prompting a CoT out of the model. Is this true? I don't remember this and looking back it appears that Google came up with it and openai was the first to release a commercial model. Dont under estimate the power of branding/positioning/marketing. For more than a year I have been using a RL'd Qwen fine tune optimised for just taking a decision and outputting the decision number, initially I didnt have much training data so after a few manual examples I asked deepseek to make them for me and had codex train it. I compared it to jev when it first came out and it was mostly neck and neck for my use case. I can't have been the only one in fact, I'm sure there must have been other people who probably even open sourced, but I couldn't find anything. I think the question going forward will be how does one keep abreast of interesting stuff happening, now that its de-coupled from direct human labour so de-bottlenecked on production capacity - just bound by how residual time/attention one has (Terence Tao was talking about this exact predicament in the latest tyler cowen podcast).The natural path of things, I suppose, is those that have a soapbox/distribution will just get larger... > Dont under estimate the power of branding/positioning/marketing.You're leaving out the UX (DX, developer experience) in this.And the better zero-shot performance when you don't have a dataset yet (could argue this falls under DX).Not to mention the faster time-to-decision and order-of-magnitude cheaper costs. I think its more like how LLMs caught everyone by surprise. A reasonable person would not think such a simple system would have been this effective, and yet here we are. Distilling that system down even further into a decision model again does not seem like it should work. But it seems to.The whole system is foreign to us, and makes us rethink what "intelligence" actually is. That's how the original Transformer architecture (LaMDA) should have been released back in the day, but Google thought it would cannibalize their search revenue. Basically there is a whole host of tarpit usage of LLMs in application backends today. This is simply another case of LLMs enabling people to build what they cannot productionize or maintain.Today developers without any AI/ML skillset can prototype a fancy new feature with LLMs, what used to require collecting and curating data to train a pipeline of ML models then serving them in production.The problem comes when it's time to take the new feature into production. That $20 cost with prototype/beta workload is now $30k per month in LLM costs, and those hallucinations that never happened on their 200 test samples is happening 600 times per day.They are then stuck, because they lack the knowledge and budget to build and run the production ML pipeline properly, the infra stack necessary to handle production workload. Management also doesn't understand why they have to invest in rebuilding something that "seems to work" with "outdated methods".These system one or decision models are a step up from LLMs when it comes to this usage. Problem is that they are still difficult to work with (limited in expression power) for many application logic. Despite the initial popularity, I hear about a lot of frictions refactoring LLM based backend with them, and multiple cases of production rollbacks to LLMs already.I think system one models is a sensible paradigm, but there is a lot more work needed above the model layer to make this work. That also makes me wonder: what other things are achieved by now and are up for grabs, and that will seem obvious in retrospect, but we don't notice it yet?Roughly speaking, has AGI actually been achieved two years ago and we go around don't noticing that? > Which makes me wonder: how do these models calculate probabilities?By unprincipled methods. To calibrate confidence in an answer you need a task specific calibration set. You can't pre-calibrate for tasks unknown ahead of time, which is the case for most uses of decision models. In some sense everything an LLM does is by unprincipled methods. But it works! We judge it empirically post hoc by its performance rather than relying on tuning.Hell, human thinking is unprincipled in basically the exact same way. We were doing zero and few-shot classification with LLMs since before they could reliably complete whole sentences. It’s an easier task than generating coherent text. The model needed to be tuned for classification (not generation) and for the domain, but it would often succeed at new classification tasks with a simple description.I guess given the huge advances in LLM since then, these models probably achieve much better accuracy on a wide range of domains with lower effort compared to what we were doing, which makes it compelling as a product. And yeah, the models probably were already good enough a few years ago too. Other factors include how easy it is to release products at high speed now, and the desire in the industry to reduce token spend. Zero-shot encoders even pre-date LLMs. People who worked in NLP in the transformers "BERT-era" may be familiar with natural language inference (NLI).Decision models are really not much different than that, but (usually) scaled up to bigger causal models.If you are looking to do Jev-like things with smaller models, check into NLI. You can do it with LLMs by looking at the logprobs of ('yes', 'Yes', 'YES'...) vs. ('no'...). This works for bool or whatever they call it in jev space nool I think?You can do it manually or use ready made libs. I know there's one in python on top of vllm that can do something like this. LLM token probabilities are really poorly calibrated for decision making.Every time I see someone saying something like "isn't this just structured output?", it's because they don't understand that probability calibration is one of the most important parts of the product, especially to understand uncertainty.I think Jev did a pretty good job on calibration. I wonder how the fast-follow competition from OpenAI and Gemini do. Right, that's always been true for LLMs + constrained generation. It ensures syntactic correctness, but semantics are "best effort". Not reliably - look at microsoft's guidance project that did some of this.Once a model goes through instruction fine tuning and RLVR/RLHF the log probs decorrelate from what's ground truth (given the propensity of the data seen during training) But I assume it wouldn't take much more training to make them good again - just a matter of picking the right loss function, since this sort of stuff is probably all encoded in the last layer or two anyway. When trying it out, OpenAI's Decisions was ~2x slower, worse accuracy and more expensive. Unless used with image-related tasks, Jev is clearly superior. I have a question about this new post, if that's okay to ask here. You wrote "if Jev says that a harmless post breaks a content policy, you cannot tell whether it reacted to a word in the post or to a sentence in the policy".How is that different from an LLM? Sure I can ask the LLM if it's because this or that word, but the LLM doesn't _know_. It will spit out something, but it doesn't mean this actually has anything to do with why it flagged the post. Sure you can remove a word and test again, but that you can obviously do with a decision model as well.Is it simply the fact that I can read through the "thought process" (assuming there is one) that makes LLM less of a black-box according to your idea? I have still not used a decision model, How are people using them at the moment? is any one using them in a coding harness like Pi? I've found that they work great as gates ("does this require a human review?") or filters ("is this suspicious?") and occasionally as judges (based on this context, is the expected pain score for this user above 7.5/10?). Interesting how do you know if it does a good job at these tasks? It seems that thinking in LLM's has been one of the things that has been so important to making sure it's a good response. It doesn't. Decision models are not more accurate than small models with no thinking. If your classification task is accuracy sensitive, you still need to stick with one of the big frontier models. Support ticket routing to a team. If the model gets it wrong, the team can put it back in the queue for manual routing. And if the model gets it wrong in the other direction, well, you didn't really need that customer anyway. I think in this example the decision is "route to team X or team Y"; so the worst-case is it ends up in the wrong teams queue, and gets moved manually. When the use case allows room for an acceptable amount of incorrect decisions because there's a manual flow those cases can be routed to still anyways. It can be used a fast/cheap router, if a response is above a specified probability then send it to LLM based workflow branch, otherwise nothing more to do I used it to classify 10k ish repos for https://hnrepos.com/I like that it’s fairly deterministic, with a bit of variation. Think very low temperature rather than perfectly repeatable. I just didn’t want the randomness that comes from token by token execution even at low temps.I’ve also used it for “does this contain an entity”, and then I run an LLM to extract the entities. Saves on the LLM cost. I'm using them to label training data for model development. You can do something like label a bunch of records with Jev, then train the model, then check results with opus and a hold-out set. I actually flipped it. Let the LLM label the records and do exploration. But the judge was Jev based. (Did the labeling meet criteria) That seems an unusual order. I guess with jev you have a confidence number and you can adjust at what confidence you decide it was good or bad. Selecting between user-provided tags to provide quick suggestions, semantic search, that sort of stuff. Task classification - given a set of classes, return the most likely class for each taskGuardrails - check the text against a set of guardrail checks (questions)Search - Given a search criteria, I first have an LLM generate a query that would go to the decision model. This query is a rubric that scores each document. The highest scoring documents become the search hits. This is fast and cheap, so you can use it as a cross-encoder for your entire set, instead of just as a final re-ranker. > How are people using them at the moment?We use it for our critique looping within our own harness.But decision models can do things like write SQL queries, if you're willing to put a little bit of trickery upfront.My team's writing a paper about it for ICDE 2027 as we speak (as a follow-up to the DICE demo/paper from VLDB 2014).But my Linkedin post[1] has a quick summary of the idea, without explaining everything we do there.[1] - https://lnkd.in/p/gAsWcrCd Tool routing. For example which MCP or Skill should i use for a given question.Evals. is this hitting the criteria or not? (Test case passes or fails) It would be awesome to be able to create mail filters using natural-ish language instead of grammar I work in manufacturing and would like to use LLMs for scenarios where there's obviously still rules for what should happen next, but there's just so many variables that I can't just code it into a decision tree easily.As an example: I could have something I'm building fail. If I take a picture of it, can I see that it's1) a false failure2) salvageable 2a) decision-tree for *who* to send it to for reworking things 3) scrapAs I think of the above decision tree, I see some problems where I'm just asking myself, "why wouldn't I just use <insert a lot of options you can probably guess here>?".I'll be honest, I think right now decision models are in a "solution looking for a problem stage", but I think there's opportunity still. My agent was stopping so jev is called each turn to see if it’s done or not - similar to how it works in Claude, according to Claude… Its bit more expensive than other other Decision Models in the same lane.However, it can accept Audio and Video as input as well and for those specific cases it can be extremely useful. Image input is a primary reason I've never moved off my "home rolled" version of Jev (that Claude wrote for me over a year ago) for my file organizer/indexer. Takes images resizes them to 1k, then asks a handful of questions about the image for tagging purposes. It is able to process around 3 images a second based on Qwen 3 VL, but distilled and optimized for 1k images and up to 2048 token inputs (after the system prompt, then the questions are asked one after each other reusing the cache). Documents that are longer than that end up going through a summarizer that runs on my other GPU (Qwen 3.6, I think). And all of that gets fed into a vector search engine, for easy lookup later.I'm not even sure what all is going on inside it anymore, because I just add new features when they popup, and tell Claude to do it, and it let's me know when it is done, and every new "input feature" can run against the entire catalogue of files. I'm trying to organize about 400k photos. What kind of questions are you asking it and what are you doing with that info? Applying tags/labels? Sorting into albums? Basically just tags, but the questions branch based on the answers. Photo vs Graphic, Portrait vs Landscape, Person/People/No one, etc.Eventually I'll add facial recognition to the photos with one or more people, but I've not felt like delving into that can of worms. Sora was a toy that only seemed to exist to infringe on IP OpenAI didn’t control. Apples and oranges. Antigravity is far superior to Jules.I say plant a thousand flowers and cull the ones that don't bloom. The difference is this is not a consumer-focused product.Google kills consumer products because most consumers don't pay for them directly, so they often end up not making enough money.With enterprise products, they have actual paying customers, so the situation is different. They just got a huge round, almost a billion in financing - that was after OAI Decisions API was released. I really wonder what their next move is. I guess it depends on how many good ideas Typesafe AI have. They never said that they were only about decision models. It’s been a little while since I’ve looked, but when the first round of jev competitors came out, jev was still significantly faster.Getting a response in 250ms opens up a lot possibilities over 750ms. Startup / Founder focus vs Large Organizations with no vision. With AI, we know distribution moat really doesn't matter and Google doesn't have a great Developer distribution moat anyway I still don't really understand where and why these decisions or Jev is useful or interesting? Is there a clear demonstration or tldr anywhere? I still have no idea why this is useful. Models are atrocious without reasoning, for classification and otherwise, and this doesn't even just eschew reasoning afaik, but parts of the models as well for lower latency and cost. I genuinely do not see the point.What differentiates this from training a classifier model? That it comes pretrained with general knowledge? I think that is exactly the value prop, you don't need to train a classifier. You get something that works well enough to validate your product/feature/whatever before investing in training. It took OpenAI 2 weeks after Jev to release a decision end point, and now google does it 2 months later. Why such a difference? Bureaucracy? Quality control? Looking at their benchmarks, it's actually a better model than OpenAI and Jev (which in the same evals is worst than Jev?). Mostly curiosity whether openAIs relative speed is more innovative and can pump out new products faster, or if they are playing fast and loose

Yes, in a sense, with some important caveats. Cross-entropy will tend to yield reasonable marginal (i.e., not class-wise, not approximately conditional) calibration for in-distribution (i.i.d. data). The challenge with LMs, and neural networks more generally, is that the resulting estimators that are based on the output logits are very brittle to covariate shifts and out-of-distribution data, and that for real applications, we often need robust estimates in high-probability regions (e.g., of class- and prediction-conditional accuracy at least some value near 1) for conditional-branching decisions (by a human or a model). (ECE is the wrong metric for that quantity.)

The various decision APIs don't give you that, and would themselves need to be recalibrated with constraints in feature-representation space over the applicable reference class, as with https://pypi.org/project/reexpress-sdm/.

blocks.html_en: The thing I had to wrap my head around is: For a "classic" classifier, the classes are fixed and the data distribution is p(x,y). The calibration is checked over this single distribution. Jev makes the tasks part of the input, so the data distribution is p(task,x,y) and calibration is averaged over that joint distribution. What follows is that while for classic classifiers, calibration brakes down if your x was out-of-distribution, it can now also break if your task is out of distribution. The big question now is: Can subtle differences in phrasing your task already lead to this? And the only way to verify calibration is having ground truth data to validate on. Also: Calibration over p(task, x, y) means calibrated on average across tasks. Even an in-distribution task can be over- or underconfident while the average looks fine.

Dont under estimate the power of branding/positioning/marketing. For more than a year I have been using a RL'd Qwen fine tune optimised for just taking a decision and outputting the decision number, initially I didnt have much training data so after a few manual examples I asked deepseek to make them for me and had codex train it. I compared it to jev when it first came out and it was mostly neck and neck for my use case. I can't have been the only one in fact, I'm sure there must have been other people who probably even open sourced, but I couldn't find anything. I think the question going forward will be how does one keep abreast of interesting stuff happening, now that its de-coupled from direct human labour so de-bottlenecked on production capacity - just bound by how residual time/attention one has (Terence Tao was talking about this exact predicament in the latest tyler cowen podcast).

The natural path of things, I suppose, is those that have a soapbox/distribution will just get larger...

Basically there is a whole host of tarpit usage of LLMs in application backends today. This is simply another case of LLMs enabling people to build what they cannot productionize or maintain.

Today developers without any AI/ML skillset can prototype a fancy new feature with LLMs, what used to require collecting and curating data to train a pipeline of ML models then serving them in production.

The problem comes when it's time to take the new feature into production. That $20 cost with prototype/beta workload is now $30k per month in LLM costs, and those hallucinations that never happened on their 200 test samples is happening 600 times per day.

They are then stuck, because they lack the knowledge and budget to build and run the production ML pipeline properly, the infra stack necessary to handle production workload. Management also doesn't understand why they have to invest in rebuilding something that "seems to work" with "outdated methods".

These system one or decision models are a step up from LLMs when it comes to this usage. Problem is that they are still difficult to work with (limited in expression power) for many application logic. Despite the initial popularity, I hear about a lot of frictions refactoring LLM based backend with them, and multiple cases of production rollbacks to LLMs already.

I think system one models is a sensible paradigm, but there is a lot more work needed above the model layer to make this work.

We were doing zero and few-shot classification with LLMs since before they could reliably complete whole sentences. It’s an easier task than generating coherent text. The model needed to be tuned for classification (not generation) and for the domain, but it would often succeed at new classification tasks with a simple description.

And yeah, the models probably were already good enough a few years ago too. Other factors include how easy it is to release products at high speed now, and the desire in the industry to reduce token spend.

Image input is a primary reason I've never moved off my "home rolled" version of Jev (that Claude wrote for me over a year ago) for my file organizer/indexer. Takes images resizes them to 1k, then asks a handful of questions about the image for tagging purposes. It is able to process around 3 images a second based on Qwen 3 VL, but distilled and optimized for 1k images and up to 2048 token inputs (after the system prompt, then the questions are asked one after each other reusing the cache). Documents that are longer than that end up going through a summarizer that runs on my other GPU (Qwen 3.6, I think). And all of that gets fed into a vector search engine, for easy lookup later.

I'm not even sure what all is going on inside it anymore, because I just add new features when they popup, and tell Claude to do it, and it let's me know when it is done, and every new "input feature" can run against the entire catalogue of files.

content_html_zh: This appears the first decision AI that actually handles audio, video, and PDF, and I'm surprised this isn't highlighted everywhere.Marketing seems to have dropped the ball on that. I doubt anyone's picking it for the +2% higher points, but being able to answer based on a PDF or call is groundbreaking.Jev is still faster and cheaper for many of the common text uses.>Marketing seems to have dropped the ball on thatGoogle's marketing consistently drops the ball on every opportunity so that's not surprising at allI'm sort of surprised it took Jev for everyone to realize "oh yeah, this is a useful thing that we should have in our product portfolio".But maybe this is one of those things that's only obvious in retrospect? I'm sure people were trying something similar years ago with grammar-constrained outputs (for example to only output a simple json structure), but you can't get probabilities out of the model that way. Which makes me wonder: how do these models calculate probabilities?A lot of AI stuff is like that, actually. GPT 2 and 3 were mainly curiosities that would get articles on tech news sites but didn’t attract much attention from the general public. But after RLHF the UX improved dramatically and ChatGPT became mainstream. A lot of MLEs underestimate how much UX matters, and the same is true for Jev.> how do these models calculate probabilities?The short answer is: more and better data.The long answer is: probably the same way any other classifier does. Take your ground truth probabilities and your predicted probabilities. The gap between those is called cross entropy, which is used to push the model towards the correct probabilities.> which is used to push the model towards the correct probabilities.The definition of "correct probability" here is usually "p=1 for the ground truth label, p=0 for all others." Which seems like an intuitive approach but if you actually think about it doesn't trivially imply the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty.Wouldn't learning a calibrated probability distribution just be a consequence of the CE loss being a proper scoring rule? So, by construction, they are approximating the distribution of the labels. Of course in practice there might be issues with overfitting the log-likelihood and the with the labels being a finite sample of the population distributionYes, in a sense, with some important caveats. Cross-entropy will tend to yield reasonable marginal (i.e., not class-wise, not approximately conditional) calibration for in-distribution (i.i.d. data). The challenge with LMs, and neural networks more generally, is that the resulting estimators that are based on the output logits are very brittle to covariate shifts and out-of-distribution data, and that for real applications, we often need robust estimates in high-probability regions (e.g., of class- and prediction-conditional accuracy at least some value near 1) for conditional-branching decisions (by a human or a model). (ECE is the wrong metric for that quantity.)The various decision APIs don't give you that, and would themselves need to be recalibrated with constraints in feature-representation space over the applicable reference class, as with https://pypi.org/project/reexpress-sdm/.For a single prediction, sure. But the model doesn't make a single prediction and then stop existing. It makes an unbounded number of future predictions and under that assumption it is reasonable to expect the model to behave optimally under Bayes rule - which has a unique global minimizer at E[(Y-F(X))^2].So counter to your claim that "It doesn't trivially imply that the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty" I think you need to consider what it means to optimally update a posterior under the global minimizer of the true conditional distribution.The thing I had to wrap my head around is: For a "classic" classifier, the classes are fixed and the data distribution is p(x,y). The calibration is checked over this single distribution. Jev makes the tasks part of the input, so the data distribution is p(task,x,y) and calibration is averaged over that joint distribution. What follows is that while for classic classifiers, calibration brakes down if your x was out-of-distribution, it can now also break if your task is out of distribution.
